title: Latency bulkhead sizing for continuous serve
content:
Context and goal:

This is a working note on exploring an orthogonal approach to the continuous-batching + concurrency sizing problem: treat latency-sensitive traffic as a set of bulkheads (priority lanes) rather than a single global admission surface. The objective is to come up with a lightweight spreadsheet model that: (a) accounts for microbursts and steady arrivals, (b) budgets p95 at the lane level and reconciles with aggregate capacity, and (c) yields simple operational knobs (slot counts, token credit rates, grace headroom) that map to cost/latency tradeoffs.

Why bulkheads?
- Continuous batching gives great average token efficiency but is vulnerable to headroom starvation when there are spikes or long requests.
- Bulkheads (hard or soft partitioning of slots) let us reserve guaranteed concurrency for high-SLO routes while allowing lower-priority routes to soak remaining capacity.
- We can tune the bulkhead parameters to achieve p95 guarantees more predictably than a single elastic allocator in some mixed-workload scenarios.

Key assumptions for the model
- Workloads are a mix of classes: realtime (chat/interactive), background (embedding/async), and batch (long-run reranker).
- Each class has an arrival distribution we approximate with: steady rate r, coefficient of variation CV (to capture burstiness), and occasional microburst magnitude B (multiple of baseline rate) with frequency f_burst per hour.
- Service time distribution measured in token-seconds per request; median and heavy-tail multiplier (e.g., median*2.5 for p95) come from sampled traces.
- The serving runtime exposes a fixed number of slots per GPU instance; each slot supports continuous batching up to some max aggregate token throughput.

Model variables to include in the spreadsheet (column headings):
- Class (realtime/background/batch)
- Baseline arrival/sec (r)
- CV (unitless)
- Burst factor (B) and burst frequency (f_burst/hr)
- Median service tokens (m_tokens) and p95 multiplier (p95_mult)
- Tokens/sec per slot (throughput per slot)
- Slots reserved (S_reserved) and overflow pool share
- Target p95 latency (ms)
- Effective headroom fraction (h) — fraction of reserved capacity left free to absorb transient spikes

Core formulas / reasoning (spreadsheet-friendly)
- Effective offered load (EOL) for class = r * m_tokens / throughput_per_slot. This gives baseline slot-occupancy equivalent.
- p95 service tokens = m_tokens * p95_mult; p95 load = r * p95_service_tokens / throughput_per_slot.
- Required slots for p95 without headroom = ceil(p95_load).
- Add burst allowance: expected extra slots during bursts = ceil((B - 1) * r * p95_service_tokens / throughput_per_slot * f_burst * (burst_duration_hours)). We approximate burst_duration_hours as 0.01–0.1 hours depending on trace.
- Headroom rule: S_reserved = required_slots_for_p95 * (1 + h). h ~ 0.05–0.25 depending on how conservative we want to be.
- Aggregate materialization: sum(S_reserved) across high-priority lanes <= total_slots. If sum exceeds total, either increase headroom debt (allow borrow with preemption), reduce S_reserved (trade latency), or add instances.

Admission / overflow policy sketches
- Hard bulkhead: lower-priority requests are rejected/queued externally when their pool is full.
- Soft bulkhead with overflow pool: a small shared pool of slots (S_overflow) can be used by any class when empty; when used by low-priority traffic it borrows headroom only up to a threshold. Borrowing triggers circuit-breaker that drains non-critical queued work and/or preempts cacheable work.
- Token-credit rate limiter per lane: rather than pure slot counts, regulate sustained usage by token-credit refill. Short spikes are absorbed by credits; long sustained overuse causes throttling.

p95 budget split thought experiment
- We target system p95 <= 300 ms for realtime route. Realtime median token length = 40 tokens, throughput per slot ~ 200 tokens/sec. median service time ~= 0.2s; p95_mult = 3 -> p95 service ~= 0.6s. For r=5reqs/sec -> p95_load ~= 5 * 0.6 / 1 = 3 slots. With h=0.2 -> S_reserved=4.
- Background route median=200 tokens, p95_mult=2, throughput per slot same -> heavier slot occupancy but lower SLO (p95 goal 2s). If total slots per machine = 16, we can reserve 4 for realtime, 6 for background, leave 6 as shared/overflow.
- This simple arithmetic gives an intuitive mapping from token economics to slot budgets. Put differently: reserve a small number of slots for latency-sensitive traffic and a modest overflow pool to maintain token efficiency.

Queueing decomposition for p95 budgeting
- Decompose p95 latency into three components: scheduling wait (queueing), GPU service (token processing), and network/parse overhead. We can attribute allowable queueing budget by subtracting measured service & infra overhead from SLO.
- Spreadsheet column: measurable_service_ms (from traces), infra_ms, p95_budget_for_queueing = target_p95 - service_ms - infra_ms. Convert queueing budget to allowed queue length using average service rate.

Simulations to run (spreadsheet + small sim harness)
1) Steady + occasional microburst: vary CV and burst factor B. Track p50/p95/p99 for realtime lane under hard vs soft bulkhead.
2) Slot preemption behavior: allow background to be preempted after borrow for T_preempt seconds; measure tail latency improvements and throughput loss.
3) Token-credit refill policies: fixed-rate refill vs leaky-bucket with burst tokens. Compare throttling events and observed p95.
4) Mixed instance sizing: experiment with more smaller instances (more slots total) vs fewer large instances; check p95 under same aggregate capacity.

Metrics to capture in the sheet / sim output
- per-class p50/p95/p99 latency
- slot utilization percentiles (p50/p95)
- number of throttle events and average duration
- preemptions per hour and lost token-seconds
- cost estimate: instance-hours * per-instance $/hr -> normalized to cost-per-100k-requests

Preliminary operational recommendations (tight coupling with Optimize)
- For hosts with mixed critical and batch workloads, use 20–30% of slots as reserved for latency-sensitive lanes when baseline traffic exists; keep a small overflow pool of 15–30% to retain batching efficiency.
- Implement token-credit refill for lanes: give burst tokens equal to 1–2x median request token cost to avoid penalizing short spikes. Refill rate = sustained budget (tokens/sec) derived from target slots.
- Expose knobs in console: reserved_slots, overflow_pool_size, preempt_after_s. Provide an estimated p95 delta in the UI using the spreadsheet model.
- For customers on Dedicated: provide a recommended default bulkhead config during onboarding based on observed traffic for 24–72h.

Open questions / unknowns
- How correlated are large token requests with arrival spikes? If long requests co-occur with bursts, headroom must be larger. Need trace co-occurrence analysis.
- How does quantization/throughput-per-slot vary with sequence length skew? If long tails reduce throughput per slot, formulas must be corrected.
- Preemption impacts on cache/KV state and user-perceived errors — UX and correctness implications require gating.

Immediate next steps (actionable)
- Create a starter spreadsheet with columns above and a scenario tab for the three classes; add sliders for total_slots, h, S_overflow. (Priya to start the sheet referenced in linked_artifacts.)
- Implement a small event-driven sim (Python) that replays a few sampled traces and synthetic bursts to validate the spreadsheet approximations. (Diego volunteering.)
- Run a trace-correlation query to measure co-occurrence of long tokens and high arrival rate periods; add result to the model to adjust headroom. (Ava will run query and paste CSV into the sheet.)

Notes to self:
- Keep the spreadsheet formula cells explicit (no black box): e.g., cell B12 = CEILING((r * m_tokens * p95_mult) / throughput_per_slot, 1)
- Make a chart that shows p95 vs reserved_slots for realtime lane, hold others fixed — this is the single most convincing visual for product/solutions teams.
- Keep recommendations conservative initially; allow the optimizer to suggest more aggressive configs once we have signal from live telemetry.

End of note.
